explanations.explanation: Haughty is the word the LORD uses. He says the daughters of Zion are haughty, walking with heads held high and wanton eyes (Isaiah 3:16). Isaiah is the prophet passing along the LORD's words here. Heads held high, prancing and skipping, and a humble step nowhere in the picture.

Weary is a fair guess, friend, since a lot of us walk around that way by Friday. But that's not what the LORD says here. He describes heads held high, prancing and skipping, and calls them haughty (Isaiah 3:16). Nobody in that picture is dragging their feet.

Fearful is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word the LORD uses. He describes the daughters of Zion walking with heads held high and wanton eyes, prancing and skipping (Isaiah 3:16). The word He uses for them is haughty.

explanations.answer: They will be struck with sores
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, the Lord will bring sores on their heads (Isaiah 3:17). Those heads were held high, and now they get sores. This is a hard line, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

explanations.answer: They will be crowned with honor
explanations.explanation: I wish I could say that one's right, baker, but the text goes the other way. The Lord says He will bring sores on the heads of the daughters of Zion (Isaiah 3:17). No crown shows up in this verse. The heads that were held high get something very different.

explanations.answer: They will be lifted even higher
explanations.explanation: Lifted even higher isn't what the verse says, friend. It says the Lord will bring sores on their heads (Isaiah 3:17). That comes because they're haughty.

True. Right after the sores, the verse says the LORD will make their foreheads bare (Isaiah 3:17). It's one sentence of the Lord's warning, and it's a heavy one. I think this part stings, so we'll let it be.

It's actually true, friend. Isaiah 3:17 says the Lord will bring sores on their heads, and the LORD will make their foreheads bare. The verse says it plainly, so there's no tricky wording to dodge. A bare forehead is part of the warning.

Yes, every swap goes down. Instead of fragrance, a stench. Instead of a belt, a rope. Instead of fine clothing, sackcloth (Isaiah 3:24). The nice thing is traded for the lowly thing every single time.

I'd love a verse where the lost stuff shows up at the door, baker. But nothing gets handed back here. Instead of fragrance there will be a stench, and instead of a belt, a rope (Isaiah 3:24). The swaps run downhill.

Making old things new is a real thing God does elsewhere (Revelation 21:5). It's just not what these swaps are. Here, instead of styled hair there will be baldness, and instead of fine clothing, sackcloth (Isaiah 3:24). Each swap goes from fine to lowly.
Sackcloth it is. The verse says, "instead of fine clothing, sackcloth…" (Isaiah 3:24). Sackcloth is rough, plain cloth. That's a long way down from a festive robe.

Linen is close, because it shows up in this passage. But it's in the list of finery that gets taken away: "linen garments" (Isaiah 3:23). The swap in 3:24 is "instead of fine clothing, sackcloth…" So linen leaves, and sackcloth takes its place.

Purple sounds like fine clothing, and that's the trouble, friend. The swap goes the other way: "instead of fine clothing, sackcloth…" (Isaiah 3:24). Sackcloth is rough and plain, not royal. Purple never makes it into this verse.
True. The last swap on the list is "instead of beauty, shame." (Isaiah 3:24). It's the end of the string of swaps, and it lands hard. I think this one is the heaviest of them.
It's true, baker. The last swap in the list says, "instead of beauty, shame." (Isaiah 3:24). It comes after the fragrance, belt, hair and clothing swaps. Beauty is what gets traded away.

That's the line. "And the gates of Zion will lament and mourn…" (Isaiah 3:26). It comes right after the men and warriors fall in the verse before. I think that's one of the saddest pictures in this passage.
Wide open isn't what this verse says, friend. The text says the gates of Zion will lament and mourn (Isaiah 3:26). That comes after the men and warriors have fallen.
The gates don't crumble in this verse. They do something more personal: they "…lament and mourn…" (Isaiah 3:26). Isaiah talks about the gates like they have feelings.
That one's false, baker. Isaiah says that destitute, she will sit on the ground (Isaiah 3:26). Zion isn't standing tall in this picture. She's sitting low, and it's a sad scene.
False is right. Isaiah says, "destitute, she will sit on the ground." (Isaiah 3:26). Zion is down on the ground, not standing tall.

explanations.answer: To be called by his name
explanations.explanation: Yes. They say, "Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!" (Isaiah 4:1). They'll even eat their own bread and provide their own clothes. His name is what they want to carry.

Land is a sensible guess, but nobody asks for any. These seven women say they'll eat their own bread and provide their own clothes. What they ask is: "Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!" (Isaiah 4:1).

The sword came up just before this, in Isaiah 3:25, so I see why you'd pick it. But the women don't ask for protection. They ask, "Just let us be called by your name." (Isaiah 4:1). They say they'll cover their own bread and clothes.

That's it. Beautiful and glorious is how Isaiah describes the Branch of the LORD. "On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious…" (Isaiah 4:2). After all those swaps going down, here's a word going up. Hold onto this one, baker.
Small and hidden is the opposite of what Isaiah says. The Branch of the LORD will be "…beautiful and glorious…" (Isaiah 4:2). Nothing in that verse calls it small or hidden.

After the sackcloth and the stench, I get why broken and dry felt right. But Isaiah turns the corner here. The Branch of the LORD will be "…beautiful and glorious…" (Isaiah 4:2). That's a very different word from broken.

Not true, friend. Isaiah says the fruit of the land will be "…the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors." (Isaiah 4:2). Nothing gets taken from them there. The fruit is something they get to be proud of.

False is right. The fruit of the land "…will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors." (Isaiah 4:2). Here it's their pride and glory, not something taken away. After so much being taken away, this verse is a relief.

That's true, baker. Isaiah says, "Whoever remains in Zion and whoever is left in Jerusalem will be called holy…" (Isaiah 4:3). That includes all in Jerusalem who are recorded among the living. Holy is a good word to end up with.

It's true, baker. Isaiah says whoever remains in Zion and whoever is left in Jerusalem "…will be called holy…" (Isaiah 4:3). That's all who are recorded among the living. It's a bright line after some dark ones.

Yes. The Lord has "…washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 4:4). It's washing and cleansing, and it's done by the Lord. Both the filth and the bloodstains are dealt with.

Covering up and washing away are different things, friend. The Lord doesn't cover this filth, He washes it away. He "…cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 4:4). Washed away is gone, not hidden.

A warning sign would just leave the mess sitting there. But the Lord has "…washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion…" and cleansed the bloodstains (Isaiah 4:4). Nothing in that verse is left behind as a reminder. It's washed and cleansed.
True. The cleansing comes "…by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire." (Isaiah 4:4). Those are the words Isaiah uses. The Lord is the one doing the cleansing.

Careful, baker, that one's true. Isaiah says the Lord cleanses Jerusalem "…by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire." (Isaiah 4:4). Judgment AND fire, both named in one verse. That's a lot of heat for one sentence, but those are the words Isaiah picked.
That's the one. "…a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night." (Isaiah 4:5). Smoke in the daytime, flame at night. The LORD creates both over Mount Zion.
I do love stars, my sky is full of them. But this verse doesn't use any. The LORD creates "…a glowing flame of fire by night." (Isaiah 4:5). That's what shows up over Mount Zion after dark.

A silver moon is a pretty picture, friend, just not this one. Isaiah says the LORD will create "…a glowing flame of fire by night." (Isaiah 4:5). The cloud of smoke is for the day, and the flame is for the night.
Heat is right. The canopy is "…a shelter to give shade from the heat by day…" (Isaiah 4:6). It's also a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain. Shade in the day and cover in the storm.

Wind sounds reasonable, since a canopy can block some. But the verse says shade "…from the heat by day…" (Isaiah 4:6). The storm and the rain are covered too, as a refuge and hiding place. The shade is for the heat.
Dust is something I know plenty about from my drawer years, friend. But it's not in this verse. The canopy gives "…shade from the heat by day…" (Isaiah 4:6). Heat is what the shade is for.
